# Lab 1: Environments as Code {.unnumbered} This lab shows how to create isolated, reproducible package environments with `renv` (R) and `venv` (Python), which every lab that follows depends on. The [first lab](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-1-env-as-code.html#lab1) includes two Quarto documents: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} _labs/lab01/ ├── eda-basic.qmd └── model-basic-py.qmd ``` ::: ## Comprehension questions > "*Why does difficulty increase as the level of required reproducibility increase for a data science project. In your day-to-day work, what’s the hardest reproducibility challenge?*" Each layer of the environment we need to reproduce adds work, and the work grows faster than the payoff. Packages are cheap to capture: `renv.lock` or `requirements.txt` records them, and one command restores them. The system layer is harder, because a lockfile can record the R version but can't install it or the operating system underneath it. At the far end, some regulated industries have to rerun an analysis exactly a decade later, which means keeping the physical hardware running. That's why the chapter calls a completely reproducible environment "a fool's errand." The hardest challenge I've run into is in the system layer. It's impossible to know what system requirements developers might need (for both Python and R), and you might not have the level of control you want on the server. > "*There’s a table of the layers of the data science environment above. It names six items across three layers. Draw a mental map of the relationships between these six items. Pay particular attention to why the higher layers depend on the lower ones.*" Each item is built for, or runs on, the item below it, so a change at the bottom reaches everything above it: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Layers of the data science environment' %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% flowchart TD subgraph PkgLayer ["Packages"] Pkgs("R + Python
packages") end subgraph SysLayer ["System"] Lang("R + Python
versions") Libs("system
libraries") OS("operating
system") end subgraph HwLayer ["Hardware"] VHw("virtual
hardware") PHw("physical
hardware") end Pkgs -->|"built for"| Lang Pkgs -->|"link to"| Libs Lang -->|"compiled for"| OS Libs -->|"compiled for"| OS OS -->|"runs on"| HwLayer VHw -->|"runs on"| PHw style Pkgs fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Lang fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Libs fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style OS fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style VHw fill:#485466,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style PHw fill:#485466,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style PkgLayer fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#D2562B,color:#1B2A41 style SysLayer fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#2A6F77,color:#1B2A41 style HwLayer fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#485466,color:#1B2A41 ``` Packages are built for a specific language version and operating system, and many of them link to system libraries (`{sf}` needs GDAL, for example). The R and Python interpreters and the system libraries are compiled for the operating system. The operating system runs on virtual hardware (an EC2 instance), and the virtual hardware runs on physical servers in a data center. Also, having old system libraries on the operating system can be enough to block R installations. > "*What are the two key attributes of environments as code? Why do you need both of them? Are there cases where you might only care about one?*" Isolation and portability. The package environment is isolated, so other work on the same machine can't disrupt it, and it can be captured and moved to another machine. These are the first two takeaways in [Project-oriented workflows](#project-oriented-workflows) below. Each one protects something different. Isolation keeps the project working when I update a package for another project. Capturing the environment lets a colleague, a server, or me in six months rebuild it. Sometimes one is enough. A throwaway analysis I'll delete next week needs isolation but not a lockfile. Inside a container, the container already provides the isolation, so the lockfile is the part I still need. > "*Draw a mental map of the relationships between the following: package repository, package library, package, project-level-library, .libPaths() (R) or sys.path (Python), lockfile.*" The `renv` and `venv` diagrams below map these items. A package repository (CRAN or PyPI) holds the current and archived versions of each package. Installing a package puts one version in a package library, which holds at most one version of each package. Libraries can be system, user, or project level, and a project-level library holds one project's packages. `.libPaths()` (R) and `sys.path` (Python) list the libraries in search order. Activating `renv` or `venv` puts the project-level library first. The lockfile (`renv.lock` or `requirements.txt`) records each package and its version, so we can rebuild the library from the repository. > "*Why is it a bad idea to share package libraries? What’s the best way to collaborate with a colleague using an environment as code? What commands will you run in R or Python to save a package environment and restore it later?*" Package installs are specific to the operating system and language version, so a library built on my laptop might not work on a colleague's machine. Package files are also large. It's much easier to share a lockfile instead: keep `renv.lock` or `requirements.txt` in Git, and each machine installs its own packages from it. In R, `renv::snapshot()` saves the environment and `renv::restore()` restores it. In Python, `python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt` saves it and `python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt` restores it. ## Project-oriented workflows Key takeaways: 1. Each project should have an **isolated** package environment that preserves the names and versions. 2. The project's dependencies/requirements should be captured in a way that **makes it exportable/transferable to another machine**.[^renv-venv] 3. Each project should have a **virtual environment** in a **standalone directory** that documents everything the project needs (usually in a GitHub or GitLab repo).[^rstats-wtf-projects] [^rstats-wtf-projects]: Read more in [What They Forgot to Teach You About R: Chapter 3, Project-oriented workflow](https://rstats.wtf/projects) [^renv-venv]: In R, this is [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html). In Python, this is [`venv`](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment). ## Virtual environments As [do4ds notes](https://do4ds.com/chapters/sec1/1-1-env-as-code.html), `venv` and `renv` "*keep user-level package caches of the actual packages and use symlinks, so only one copy of the package is installed.*" ### `renv` First, read the documentation on [project level management with `renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/index.html) and [using renv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-renv). I’ve summarized the steps below: 1. Create a new R project-local environment ```r install.packages("renv") renv::init() ``` 2. Install packages into the renv-managed environment ```r install.packages(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2")) ``` 3. Snapshot the state of the environment and package versions in the lock file (`renv.lock`) ```r renv::snapshot() ``` 4. To deactivate the environment, close the R session. `renv` projects are automatically reactivated the next time the project is opened. Restore the environment on a new system with: ```r renv::restore() ``` #### The `renv-eda-basic` project To demonstrate how to use `renv`, I've copied the `eda-basic.qmd` file into its own project folder (`renv-eda-basic`): ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} _labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/ └── eda-basic.qmd ``` ::: Then I ran `renv::init()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::init() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Initiating `renv` in a project root directory will create the `.Rprofile` and `renv.lock` files and a `renv/` folder: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} _labs/lab01/renv-eda-basic/ ├── .Rprofile ├── .gitignore ├── eda-basic.qmd ├── renv │ ├── .gitignore │ ├── activate.R │ └── settings.json ├── renv-eda-basic.Rproj └── renv.lock ``` ::: The `renv-eda-basic.Rproj` file comes from RStudio, not `renv::init()`. It helps enforce project-oriented workflows (but `.Rproj` files are specific to RStudio). To install the packages, we can use `install.packages()` or `pak::pak()` for more flexible installations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("pak") pak::pak(c("tidyverse", "shiny", "ggplot2")) ``` ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [**Note**]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} In an `renv` project, `install.packages()` calls `renv::install()`, which uses cached packages when available. Otherwise, it installs the latest version from CRAN. ::: :::: Create a snapshot (i.e., the current versions of R and any installed packages, along with the R repositories) with `renv::snapshot()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::snapshot() ``` ::: The dependencies are saved in the `renv.lock` file, which should be committed to version control. To make sure the dependencies in the `renv.lock` file have been installed (i.e., after cloning), run: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} renv::restore() ``` ::: The diagram below maps how packages flow between CRAN, the `renv` cache, the project library, and the lockfile: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'renv' %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% flowchart TD %% External sources CRAN("CRAN/
GitHub/...") %% Local components SysLib("system
library") ProjLib("project
library") RenvCache[("renv
cache")] Lockfile[("lockfile")] %% Subgraph for "your computer" vs "the internet" subgraph Internet ["Internet"] CRAN end subgraph Computer ["Computer"] SysLib ProjLib RenvCache Lockfile end %% Connections with function labels SysLib -->|"init()"| ProjLib CRAN -->|"install()
update()"| RenvCache RenvCache -->|"renv"| ProjLib ProjLib <-->|"status()"| Lockfile ProjLib -->|"snapshot()"| Lockfile Lockfile -->|"restore()"| ProjLib %% styling %% classDef default fill:#F2E6C2,stroke:#2A6F77,color:#1B2A41 style CRAN fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style SysLib fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style RenvCache fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style ProjLib fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Lockfile fill:#485466,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Internet fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#5B8C5A,color:#1B2A41 style Computer fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#2A6F77,color:#1B2A41 ``` ### `venv` Read the [documentation on Python virtual environments](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/guides/installing-using-pip-and-virtual-environments/#creating-a-virtual-environment) and using [venv with Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/virtual-environments.html#using-venv). I've summarized the steps below: 1. Create new Python 3 virtual environment in the `.venv` directory ```bash python3 -m venv .venv ``` 2. Activate the environment ```bash source .venv/bin/activate ``` 3. Use `pip` to install packages into your environment ```bash python3 -m pip install jupyter matplotlib pandas ``` 4. Deactivate an environment ```bash deactivate ``` 5. Save environment ```bash python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt ``` 6. Restoring environment ```bash python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt ``` #### The `venv-model-basic-py` project Use the **Terminal** to navigate to the `venv-model-basic-py` folder and create the Python virtual environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} python3 -m venv .venv ``` ::: This will create a `.venv/` folder inside `venv-model-basic-py`. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} _labs/lab01/venv-model-basic-py/ ├── .venv │ ├── bin │ ├── include │ ├── lib │ └── pyvenv.cfg └── model-basic-py.qmd ``` ::: To activate the virtual environment, run the following in the **Terminal**: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} source .venv/bin/activate ``` ::: This should change the **Terminal** prompt from: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$ ``` ::: to: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} (.venv) Bash@MacBook venv-model-basic-py$ ``` ::: Now we can install the required Python packages (we include `jupyter` for interactive outputs): ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} pip install palmerpenguins pandas numpy scikit-learn jupyter ``` ::: To store the installed packages, save them to a `requirements.txt` file with `pip freeze`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} python3 -m pip freeze > requirements.txt ``` ::: The diagram below maps how packages flow between PyPI, the `pip` cache, the virtual environment, and `requirements.txt`: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'venv' %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%% flowchart TD %% External sources PyPI("PyPI/
GitHub/...") %% Local components SysPython("system
Python") VirtEnv("virtual
environment") PipCache[("pip
cache")] Requirements[("requirements.txt")] %% Subgraph for "your computer" vs "the internet" subgraph Internet ["Internet"] PyPI end subgraph Computer ["Computer"] SysPython VirtEnv PipCache Requirements end %% Connections with function labels SysPython -->|"python -m venv"| VirtEnv PyPI -->|"pip install
pip install -U"| PipCache PipCache -->|"pip"| VirtEnv VirtEnv <--->|"pip list
pip show"| Requirements VirtEnv -->|"pip freeze"| Requirements Requirements -->|"pip install -r"| VirtEnv %% Additional workflow arrows VirtEnv -.->|"source activate
deactivate"| VirtEnv %% Styling style PyPI fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style SysPython fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style VirtEnv fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style PipCache fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Requirements fill:#485466,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff style Internet fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#5B8C5A,color:#1B2A41 style Computer fill:#fbf7ec,stroke:#2A6F77,color:#1B2A41 ``` #### Rendering with Python To render, use the following in the **Terminal**: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} quarto preview model-basic-py.qmd --no-browser --no-watch-inputs ``` ::: Quarto uses the first Python on the `PATH`, so rendering with the virtual environment active uses `.venv`. Or we can set the Python interpreter with the `QUARTO_PYTHON` environment variable in the **Terminal**:[^venv-win] ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} export QUARTO_PYTHON="${PWD}/.venv/bin/python3" ``` ::: [^venv-win]: On Windows try `.venv\Scripts\python.exe` If you're working inside **RStudio or Posit Workbench**, consider letting `reticulate` manage the Python environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(reticulate) use_virtualenv("myenv", required = TRUE) virtualenv_install( envname = "myenv", packages = c("palmerpenguins", "pandas", "numpy", "scikit-learn", "jupyter")) ``` ::: This ensures RStudio uses a known-good Python environment. Now, if we open the `model-basic-py.qmd` file in RStudio and click the **Render** button in the toolbar we should see the rendered output. ## Recap 1. Each project gets its own isolated, transferable package environment. In R, `renv::init()` creates the project library and `renv.lock`, `renv::snapshot()` records the package versions, and `renv::restore()` reinstalls them on another machine. 2. In Python, `python3 -m venv .venv` creates the environment and `source .venv/bin/activate` turns it on. `pip freeze > requirements.txt` captures the installed packages, and `pip install -r requirements.txt` restores them. 3. Quarto has to be told which Python interpreter to use. We can render with the virtual environment active, set `QUARTO_PYTHON` to `.venv/bin/python3` in the Terminal, or let `reticulate` manage the environment inside RStudio. Next, [Modeling in Python](model-basic-py.qmd) walks through the code in `model-basic-py.qmd`.
